q: A biological molecule is a chemical compound that naturally occurs in ______.
e: Biological molecules are defined as compounds that naturally occur in living organisms.

q: Carbon is an element present in all ______ biological molecules.
e: All organic biological molecules contain carbon.

q: Macromolecules made of long chains of monomers held together by chemical bonds are known as ______.
e: Polymers are macromolecules composed of repeating monomer units linked by chemical bonds.

q: Which of the following is NOT a polymer?
e: Lipids are important biomolecules but are not polymers because they are not made of repeating monomer units.

q: Water typically forms between ______ of the mass of most cells.
e: Water is a major component of cells, usually making up 70–95% of their mass.

q: In human cells, water is present at approximately ______.
e: About 60% of the human body (and thus human cells) is composed of water.

q: Water molecules are polar because ______.
a: oxygen has a slight negative charge and hydrogen has a slight positive charge
hydrogen has a slight negative charge and oxygen has a slight positive charge
e: The polarity of water arises from the partial negative charge on oxygen and partial positive charges on hydrogen atoms.

q: The bond formed between water molecules due to their polarity is called a ______.
e: Hydrogen bonds form between the slightly positive hydrogen of one water molecule and the slightly negative oxygen of another.

q: Water has a high specific heat, which means it ______.
a: absorbs a lot of heat with little temperature change
e: High specific heat allows water to absorb large amounts of heat while resisting temperature changes.

q: The property of water that allows sweat to cool the body is its ______.
e: Evaporating sweat removes significant heat due to water’s high heat of vaporization.

q: Water is called the universal solvent because it dissolves ______.
e: Due to its polarity, water dissolves all polar and ionic substances, making it the universal solvent.

q: Cohesion in water refers to the tendency of water molecules to ______.
e: Cohesion is the attraction between like molecules—in this case, water molecules sticking to one another.

q: Adhesion of water contributes to ______ in plants.
e: Adhesion—the attraction of water to different surfaces—helps drive capillary action in plant xylem.

q: The density of water is highest at ______.
e: Water reaches maximum density at 4°C; below this, it expands as it freezes.

q: Ice floats on liquid water because ______.
a: it is denser than liquid water
it is less dense than liquid water
e: Solid water (ice) is less dense than liquid water, so it floats—an unusual property critical for aquatic life.

q: Carbohydrates are composed of ______.
e: Carbohydrates consist of carbon (C), hydrogen (H), and oxygen (O).

q: The general formula for monosaccharides is ______.
e: Monosaccharides follow the general formula $C_nH_{2n}O_n$, such as glucose ($C_6H_{12}O_6$).

q: Triose sugars have ______ carbon atoms.
e: Triose sugars, like glyceraldehyde, contain three carbon atoms.

q: Pentose sugars include ______, which are components of nucleic acids.
e: Ribose (in RNA) and deoxyribose (in DNA) are pentose sugars essential for nucleic acid structure.

q: Hexose sugars have the general formula ______.
e: Hexose sugars like glucose and fructose have the molecular formula $C_6H_{12}O_6$.

q: Glucose exists in two ring isomers known as ______.
e: Glucose forms α-glucose and β-glucose isomers based on the orientation of the hydroxyl group.

q: Disaccharides are formed when two monosaccharides join via a ______.
e: A glycosidic linkage (covalent bond) connects two monosaccharides to form a disaccharide.

q: Maltose is composed of ______.
e: Maltose consists of two glucose units linked together.

q: Sucrose is made up of ______.
e: Sucrose (table sugar) is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose.

q: Lactose is a disaccharide found in ______.
e: Lactose is the sugar naturally present in milk, composed of glucose and galactose.

q: Polysaccharides are ______ in water.
e: Polysaccharides like starch, glycogen, and cellulose are generally insoluble in water.

q: Cellulose is made of ______ subunits.
e: Cellulose consists of β-glucose units linked by β-1,4-glycosidic bonds.

q: Starch is composed of ______.
e: Starch includes both linear amylose and branched amylopectin, both made of α-glucose.

q: Amylose contains ______ glycosidic linkages.
e: Amylose is a linear chain of α-glucose units joined by α-1,4 glycosidic linkages.

q: Amylopectin differs from amylose because it has ______.
e: Amylopectin is branched, with α-1,4 links in chains and α-1,6 links at branch points.

q: Glycogen is the main storage carbohydrate in ______.
e: Glycogen is stored in animal liver and muscle cells and in fungi.

q: Compared to amylopectin, glycogen has branches ______.
e: Glycogen is more highly branched than amylopectin, with branches every ~10 glucose units.

q: Lipids are composed of ______.
e: Triglycerides (common lipids) consist of one glycerol and three fatty acid molecules.

q: Fatty acids in simple lipids usually contain ______ carbon atoms.
e: Most fatty acids in biological lipids have 12 to 22 carbon atoms.

q: Plant lipids are often ______ fats.
e: Plant oils are typically unsaturated fats, which are considered healthier than saturated fats.

q: Animal lipids (except fish oil) are often ______ fats.
e: Most animal fats are saturated, which can pose health risks if consumed excessively.

q: Lipids store more energy per gram than ______.
e: Lipids yield more than twice the energy per gram compared to carbohydrates or proteins.

q: A layer of fat under the skin provides ______.
e: Subcutaneous fat reduces heat loss, acting as thermal insulation.

q: Lipids help aquatic animals float because they are ______ than water.
e: Lipids are less dense than water, contributing to buoyancy in marine animals.

q: Proteins are formed by joining many ______ with peptide bonds.
e: Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, linked by peptide bonds.

q: A peptide bond forms between the ______ of one amino acid and the ______ of another.
e: Peptide bonds are covalent bonds between the –NH₂ (amine) group and –COOH (carboxyl) group.

q: There are about ______ naturally occurring amino acids.
e: Approximately 20 standard amino acids combine to form all proteins in living organisms.

q: The linear sequence of amino acids in a protein is its ______ structure.
e: The primary structure is the specific order of amino acids in the polypeptide chain.

q: The α-helix and β-pleated sheet are examples of ______ protein structure.
e: Secondary structure involves local folding into α-helices or β-sheets due to backbone interactions.

q: Tertiary structure results primarily from interactions between ______.
e: Tertiary folding is driven by interactions among the R (side) groups of amino acids.

q: Haemoglobin exhibits ______ protein structure.
e: Haemoglobin consists of four polypeptide chains, giving it quaternary structure.

q: When a protein loses its shape due to heat or pH change, it is said to be ______.
e: Denaturation is the irreversible loss of protein structure and function due to disruption of bonds.

q: Enzymes are mostly ______ that act as catalysts.
e: Most enzymes are proteins that speed up biochemical reactions without being consumed.

q: Many enzyme names end in ______.
e: Enzyme names commonly end with the suffix '-ase', e.g., amylase, lipase.

q: The specific region on an enzyme where the substrate binds is called the ______.
e: The active site is the precise location where substrate binding and catalysis occur.

q: The 'lock and key model' describes the ______ between enzyme and substrate.
e: This model illustrates how only a specifically shaped substrate fits into the enzyme’s active site.

q: A non-protein helper molecule required by some enzymes is called a ______.
e: Cofactors (inorganic ions or organic coenzymes) assist enzyme function.

q: NAD is an example of a ______ derived from vitamin B complex.
e: NAD (Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide) is a coenzyme involved in cellular respiration.

q: Deficiency of vitamin C causes ______.
e: Scurvy, characterized by bleeding gums and poor wound healing, results from vitamin C deficiency.

q: Vitamin D helps bones absorb ______.
e: Vitamin D promotes calcium and phosphate uptake, essential for bone health.

q: Nucleic acids contain the elements carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and ______.
e: Phosphorus is a key component of the phosphate group in nucleotides.

q: The two main types of nucleic acids are ______.
e: DNA stores genetic information; RNA helps translate it into proteins.

q: Each nucleotide contains a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar, and a ______.
e: Nucleotides consist of a phosphate group, a 5-carbon sugar, and a nitrogenous base.

q: Adenine and guanine are classified as ______.
e: Purines (adenine and guanine) have a double-ring structure.

q: Cytosine and thymine are ______.
e: Pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine in DNA; uracil in RNA) have a single-ring structure.

q: RNA contains ______ instead of thymine.
e: In RNA, uracil replaces thymine as the complementary base to adenine.

q: DNA is ______ stranded, while RNA is ______ stranded.
e: DNA forms a double helix; RNA is typically single-stranded.

q: The pentose sugar in DNA is ______.
e: DNA contains deoxyribose (lacking one oxygen atom compared to ribose in RNA).

q: The cell membrane is also called the ______.
e: The plasma membrane surrounds the cell and regulates substance movement.

q: The plasma membrane is primarily made of a bilayer of ______.
e: Phospholipids form the fundamental bilayer structure of the cell membrane.

q: In phospholipids, the phosphate head is ______.
e: The phosphate head is hydrophilic (water-attracting) and faces the aqueous environments.

q: The fatty acid tails of phospholipids are ______.
e: Fatty acid tails are hydrophobic (water-repelling) and face inward in the bilayer.

q: Cholesterol in animal cell membranes helps to ______.
e: Cholesterol prevents the membrane from becoming too rigid or too fluid.

q: Integral proteins may function as ______ in the membrane.
e: Integral proteins often serve as transport channels or active pumps.

q: Carbohydrates on the cell surface are attached to proteins or lipids to form ______.
e: Surface carbohydrates form glycoproteins (with proteins) or glycolipids (with lipids).

q: Carbohydrates on the cell membrane are important for ______.
e: Membrane carbohydrates act as identity markers for cell-cell recognition.

q: Passive transport does NOT require ______.
e: Passive transport relies on kinetic energy and gradients, not cellular energy (ATP).

q: Diffusion is the movement of molecules from ______.
e: Diffusion moves substances down their concentration gradient—from high to low concentration.

q: Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the membrane by ______.
e: These small nonpolar gases diffuse directly through the lipid bilayer.

q: Facilitated diffusion uses ______ to transport substances.
e: Channel or carrier proteins enable facilitated diffusion without energy expenditure.

q: Glucose enters red blood cells via ______.
e: Glucose is hydrophilic and requires channel proteins for facilitated diffusion.

q: Osmosis is the net movement of ______ through a partially permeable membrane.
e: Osmosis specifically refers to water movement down a water potential gradient.

q: Water potential is higher in a ______ solution.
e: Dilute solutions have more free water molecules, hence higher water potential.

q: In a hypertonic solution, an animal cell will ______.
e: Water leaves the cell in hypertonic conditions, causing shrinkage (crenation).

q: In a hypotonic solution, a plant cell becomes ______.
e: Water enters the plant cell, creating turgor pressure against the rigid cell wall.

q: Plasmolysis occurs when a plant cell is placed in a ______ solution.
e: In hypertonic solutions, water leaves the plant cell, causing cytoplasm to pull away from the wall.

q: Active transport moves substances ______ the concentration gradient.
e: Active transport requires energy to move solutes from low to high concentration.

q: Active transport requires ______.
e: Carrier proteins use ATP energy to pump substances against their gradient.

q: Cyanide stops active transport by inhibiting ______.
e: Cyanide halts cellular respiration, preventing ATP synthesis needed for active transport.

q: Phagocytosis is also known as ______.
e: Phagocytosis involves engulfing large solid particles like bacteria.

q: Pinocytosis is the uptake of ______.
e: Pinocytosis ('cell drinking') internalizes extracellular fluid and solutes.

q: Exocytosis is used for ______.
e: Exocytosis expels waste or secretes substances like hormones or mucus.

q: Endocytosis and exocytosis involve the formation of ______.
e: Both processes use membrane-bound vesicles to move materials in or out of the cell.
